title: Intersecting Chords Theorem (Euclid III.35)
content:
The **Product of Segments of Chords** theorem states that when two chords of a circle intersect at a point P:

$$PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$$

This elegant result says that the product of the segments is the same for *any* chord through P. The product depends only on P's position relative to the circle, not on which direction the chord goes. This is Wiedijk's 100 Theorems #55.

title: Circle and On-Circle Definitions
content: Defines a circle in $\mathbb{R}^2$ as a structure with center $O$, radius $r > 0$, and the predicate `onCircle P C` meaning $\|P - O\| = r$. The `Vec2` abbreviation uses Mathlib's `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)`, providing inner product operations needed for the algebraic proof approach.

title: Power of a Point
content: The **power of a point** P with respect to a circle is $\text{pow}(P) = \|PO\|^2 - r^2$. This is the central invariant of the proof: it is independent of the chord direction. Two lemmas establish its sign behavior: `power_neg_inside` shows pow(P) < 0 for interior points (using `sq_lt_sq'`), and `abs_power_inside` gives $|\text{pow}(P)| = r^2 - \|PO\|^2$.
mathContext: $\text{pow}(P) = \|PO\|^2 - r^2$; for $P$ inside the circle: $|\text{pow}(P)| = r^2 - \|PO\|^2 > 0$

title: Chord Points Satisfy a Quadratic Equation
content: Key lemma parametrizing chord intersections with the circle. A point $Q(t) = P + t \cdot \vec{d}$ (with $\|\vec{d}\| = 1$) lies on a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin iff $t^2 + 2t\langle P, \vec{d}\rangle + (\|P\|^2 - r^2) = 0$. This quadratic in $t$ has exactly two roots $t_1, t_2$ (the two intersection points of the chord with the circle). The proof expands $\|P + t\vec{d}\|^2 = r^2$ using `inner_add_left`, `inner_add_right`, `inner_smul_left`, `inner_smul_right` and simplifies with $\langle \vec{d}, \vec{d}\rangle = 1$.
mathContext: $t^2 + 2t\langle P, \vec{d}\rangle + (\|P\|^2 - r^2) = 0$, a monic quadratic with constant term equal to the power

title: Vieta's Formulas: Root Product = Power of Point
content: The proof's algebraic core: by Vieta's formulas, the product of roots of $t^2 + bt + c = 0$ equals $c$. Here $c = \|P\|^2 - r^2$, so $t_1 \cdot t_2 = \|P\|^2 - r^2 = \text{pow}(P)$. The proof derives this without explicitly invoking Vieta: it subtracts the two instances of the quadratic to get the sum $t_1 + t_2 = -2\langle P, \vec{d}\rangle$, then uses the identity $(t_1+t_2)^2 = t_1^2 + 2t_1 t_2 + t_2^2$ to extract the product. This is more elementary than using Vieta directly but requires careful algebraic manipulation.
mathContext: $t_1 \cdot t_2 = \|P\|^2 - r^2$; derived from $t_1 + t_2 = -2\langle P, \vec{d}\rangle$ and the sum-of-squares identity

title: Interior Points: Opposite Signs and Absolute Values
content: For a point inside the circle ($\|P\| < r$), the chord parameters $t_1, t_2$ have opposite signs (the point separates the two intersection points). This follows from $t_1 t_2 = \|P\|^2 - r^2 < 0$. The algebraic product theorem then gives $|t_1| \cdot |t_2| = r^2 - \|P\|^2$, converting signed parameters to distances. The proof uses `abs_mul` and `abs_of_neg` to handle the sign.

title: Product of Segments of Chords (Main Theorem)
content: The main theorem in full generality: for a circle with any center (not just the origin), if chords AB and CD intersect at interior point P, then $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$. The proof is a two-line application of `power_of_point_product`: both products equal $|\text{pow}(P)|$, so they are equal. The translation to arbitrary center is handled by `power_of_point_product`, which works with general circles.

title: Power of Point Equals Product of Distances
content: The crucial bridge lemma: $PA \cdot PB = |\text{pow}(P)|$ for any chord through $P$. The proof translates to center-at-origin coordinates ($P' = P - O$, $A' = A - O$), parameterizes the chord using a unit direction vector $\vec{d} = (A'-P')/\|A'-P'\|$, and applies the chord quadratic analysis. The main computation shows $|t| \cdot \|A'-P'\|^2 = |\|P'\|^2 - r^2|$ by deriving Vieta's product formula for the parametric roots. This is the longest proof in the file (~160 lines) because it handles coordinate translation, normalization, and all the algebraic bookkeeping.

title: Special Case: P at the Center
content: When $P$ is at the center of the circle, every chord through $P$ is a diameter. Both segments have length $r$, so $PA \cdot PB = r^2$. The proof uses the diameter condition $A + B = 2O$ and the on-circle conditions $\|A - O\| = \|B - O\| = r$. This confirms $|\text{pow}(O)| = |0 - r^2| = r^2$, the maximum product for any interior point.
mathContext: $P = O \implies PA \cdot PB = r \cdot r = r^2$ (maximum value)

title: Converse: Equal Products Imply Concyclic Points
content: The converse theorem states: if $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$ for lines through $P$, then $A, B, C, D$ lie on a common circle. This is axiomatized because a full proof requires constructing the circumcircle of three points (e.g., $A, B, C$) and then showing $D$ lies on it via the power invariant. The axiom is the file's sole assumption, keeping `axiomCount: 1`.
mathContext: $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD \implies A, B, C, D$ are concyclic

title: Numerical Verification Examples
content: Three concrete examples verified by `norm_num`: (1) Circle of radius 5, P at distance 3: $PA \cdot PB = 25 - 9 = 16$. (2) Equal products $2 \times 8 = 4 \times 4$: the second chord is bisected at P. (3) Asymmetric case: $1 \times 12 = 2 \times 6$. These serve as sanity checks and illustrate the theorem's predictive power.
